Thursday, 17 October 2029. The regional TV programme “Lyon Soir” invites Julien and Inès (12) onto the set. It is the first time Inès has spoken on television, live.

Good evening and welcome to “Lyon Soir”. Tonight’s top story: “Inauguration of the Hélène Morel hall: one month on, what’s the verdict?” Our guests: Julien Moreau, conductor, and Inès, clarinettist. Inès, do you have stage fright?
A little. My mum told me not to look at the camera. But I’m looking at it anyway.
(laughs) Julien, the papers have talked about you a lot. First a fake news story, then a very moving inauguration. What has changed since?
Many things. On the one hand, we’ve received more than two hundred applications. On the other hand, three schools in the region have asked us to help them create their own orchestra.
Two hundred! Admittedly, that’s a success. But do you have room for everyone?
No, and that’s our problem. Although the hall is big, we can only take sixty children. On the other hand, we can share our method.
Inès, they say your clarinet has a story. Is it true?
Yes. It was given by Mrs Roux. It belonged to her husband, Lucien. He played in a brass band in Villeurbanne. Mrs Roux says he watches over me from up there. So I’m not allowed to play out of tune.
Julien, there’s a rumour going round. The orchestra has reportedly been invited to play in Paris. Do you confirm?

(smiles) This time, I confirm. This morning we received a letter from the Philharmonie de Paris. The orchestra has been invited to play on 6 April, during a festival of children’s orchestras. The children don’t know yet. Inès, you’re the first.
(silence) In Paris? For real? On TV you can’t lie, right?
Live, in front of a hundred thousand viewers? No, I can’t lie.
Well, there’s our headline for tomorrow: “La Duchère children invited to Paris”. Inès, a last word for our viewers?
Yes. Mum, I looked at the camera. Sorry. But it was for a good reason.

The day after the programme, Inès had become famous. At the La Duchère market, the vegetable seller gave her a free apple. At school, pupils she didn’t know asked for her autograph in their exercise books. And on the bus, an old lady looked at her for a long time before saying: “You were right to look at the camera, my dear.”

Her mother, on the other hand, didn’t smile straight away. She spent the evening explaining to the whole family, on the phone, that no, her daughter was not badly brought up, and yes, she was going to play in Paris. Then, around midnight, she cut out the Lyon Matin article and stuck it on the fridge door, next to the school reports.

Her teacher, Mrs Lefort, took the opportunity to give a lesson about the press. She brought five different newspapers and asked the pupils to compare the headlines. “La Duchère children invited to Paris,” said one. “A twelve-year-old clarinettist steals the show,” said another. “You see?” the teacher explained. “It’s the same information. Yet each paper tells a different story.” Inès raised her hand: “And which one is right?” The teacher smiled: “That’s for you to decide. That’s why you have to read several.”

But the joy didn’t last long. The following Monday, Claire Vasseur gathered Julien, Ioana and Radu in her office. On the table was a sheet covered in figures. She looked tired. “I’ve done the sums,” she said. “Sixty children, twenty adults, the train, two nights in a hotel, meals, insurance. Eighteen thousand euros.”

There was a long silence. “And how much can the Conservatoire pay?” Julien asked. Claire shook her head. “Three thousand, maybe four. This year’s budget has already been voted. And although I’m the director, I can’t invent money. Mr Delorme said it on the radio: there’s no magic money.”

“Delorme’s cheque pays for the coach to the station,” Radu calculated. “That’s something. But we’re still fourteen thousand euros short.” Ioana looked out of the window. On the banks of the Saône, the plane-tree leaves were falling. “How much time do we have left?” “Until the end of December,” Claire replied. “After that, the train tickets will be too expensive.”

That same evening, Julien gathered the parents in the Hélène Morel hall. He hid nothing. He wrote the figures on the board, like a maths teacher, and waited for the reactions. They didn’t take long. One father suggested cancelling. “Paris is for rich people,” he said. “Our children will play in Lyon. That’s already very good.”

Mrs Mansouri stood up. Her arms were still crossed, but her voice was calm. “Admittedly, fourteen thousand euros is a lot. But how many of us are there in the neighbourhood? Ten thousand? That’s one euro forty per person. I spend more than that on mint tea every week.” The whole hall laughed, even the father who wanted to cancel.

That was how the idea of the big La Duchère Christmas market was born. On the one hand, families would make cakes and dishes from all the countries of the neighbourhood. On the other hand, the orchestra would give little concerts all day, in front of the hall, under the lime tree. All the money would go to the trip.

Marc Delorme wrote three articles in the neighbourhood paper. The first was simply called: “Fourteen thousand euros, sixty dreams.” It was well written, fair and without exaggeration. Pierre Duval read it and quoted it in Lyon Matin. “That boy has talent,” he told Radu. “Pity he discovered it this way.”

Marc’s second article told the story of Lucien Roux’s clarinet, and the third that of Yanis’s red cello. Mrs Roux bought ten copies of the paper and handed them out to all her neighbours. “That young man writes well,” she told anyone who would listen. “Although he did something stupid, he has a good heart. Lucien did stupid things too, at his age. He even stole a trumpet once. He gave it back the next day.”

Meanwhile, Radu had another problem, a more personal one. One Sunday evening, Lucia announced that she had found the ideal place for the wedding party. “The Hélène Morel hall,” she said, her eyes shining. “With the children’s orchestra. And the lime tree in front. Imagine the photos!” Radu put down his fork. He didn’t answer straight away.

“I can’t,” he said in the end. “Do you realise? Two months ago, a journalist wrote that I got the project thanks to my sister. If I hold my wedding in that hall, people will say I built it for myself.” Lucia looked at him as if he had said something enormously stupid. Which, according to her, was exactly the case.

The next day Radu talked about it to Ioana, at the office, hoping she would be on his side. She listened to the end, then picked up a pencil, as always when she was thinking. “It’s true that people talk,” she said. “Nevertheless, you can’t live according to what a liar might say.”

“First, the town hall rents the hall to any resident who asks. You’ll pay like everyone else, and you’ll keep the invoice. Next, if the children play at your wedding, you’ll make a donation for the Paris trip. Finally, Lucia is right: there is no lovelier place in Lyon. That’s why you’re going to call her right now and say yes.”

Radu called Lucia and said yes. She shrieked so loudly that Ioana heard her from the other side of the office. Then Radu called the town hall, filled in the form and paid the rent, like everyone else. He kept the invoice in an envelope on which he wrote in big letters: “For Mr Marc D., just in case.”

A few days later, Lucia got a message from Seville. Don Manuel and doña Carmen had booked their plane tickets for 1 May. Doña Carmen had set one condition: she wanted a window seat, so she could pray while looking at the clouds. Don Manuel, for his part, asked whether he could take his guitar into the cabin. “I’m not putting it in the hold,” he wrote. “It’s sixty years old. It’s more afraid of planes than your grandmother.”

The big Christmas market took place on Saturday 14 December. It was cold, a dry blue cold, and the sky was perfectly clear. From eight in the morning, tables had been set up all around the hall. There were gazelle horns and makrouds, crêpes, empanadas, baklavas, mulled wine and mint tea.

From Iași, Ioana’s grandmother had posted a five-kilo parcel: four cozonacs, a jar of plum jam and a letter in French, written with Radu’s help over the phone. “For the children of Paris,” said the letter. The cozonacs sold out in twenty minutes. People kept coming back for more, and Ioana had to explain there were none left.

From Annecy, Pierre Moreau, Julien’s father, had come in his baker’s van, full of brioches and walnut bread. Brigitte ran the till with Manon, who sang Christmas songs between customers. Odile was selling scarves she had knitted all autumn, forty-two scarves, all in different colours.

Every hour, the orchestra played three pieces under the lime tree. The children wore woolly hats and fingerless gloves. Mihaela played the țambal with a coat over her shoulders. Mr Mansouri had brought his oud, and Yanis, for the first time, played a duet with his father. They had rehearsed in secret for a month, at night, when his father came home from work.

Mrs Mansouri, who knew nothing about the duet, dropped the tray of glasses she was holding. Nobody looked at the broken glasses. Everyone was watching the father and the son, the oud and the cello, answering each other like two people who had finally found a common language.

Around four, a man in a grey suit stopped in front of Odile’s table. It was Bernard Delorme. He looked at the scarves for a long time without saying anything, then bought ten, one of each colour. “For my grandchildren,” he explained. “And for the city council. It’s cold in the council chamber.” Odile gave him his change, looking him straight in the eye. “You know, sir, my husband rarely changed his mind either. But when he did, it was for ever.”

At six in the evening, when night had fallen, Claire Vasseur counted the money in the hall, with Radu and two mothers. They counted once, then a second time, to be sure. Nine thousand three hundred euros. It was enormous. It was more than they had ever hoped for. Yet they were still almost five thousand euros short.

Julien didn’t want to tell the children that evening. He didn’t want to spoil the party. He only said they had made great progress, which was true. The children went home tired and happy, their fingers frozen and their pockets full of cakes. The adults, on the other hand, went home doing sums in their heads.

Three days later, a letter arrived at the Conservatoire. It had no sender’s name. Inside was a cheque for five thousand euros, and a card with a single sentence, written in blue ink, in a slanting, careful hand: “My aunt would have wanted the children to see Paris.”

Claire understood at once. There was only one person who could write “my aunt” about Hélène: Pierre Garnier, the instrument dealer on rue des Tables-Claudiennes, the one who had sold Julien the piano years before. He had just sold Hélène’s little flat in Fourvière.

Julien went to thank him that same day. Mr Garnier was in his shop, repairing an old violin. He pretended not to understand. “A cheque? What cheque?” he said without looking up. “I don’t know what you’re talking about.” Then he added, still without looking up: “But if it were me, I’d say that Hélène taught me to play the piano when I was six. And that I never thanked her.”

The last rehearsal before Christmas took place on Wednesday 18 December. Julien let the children play the waltz to the end. Then he put down his score and said, simply: “We have the money. On 6 April, we play in Paris.” He couldn’t say any more, because sixty children threw themselves on him at once.

When calm had returned, Yanis raised his hand, as at school. “Sir, in Paris, will there be a window in the ceiling?” Julien smiled. “No, Yanis. The Philharmonie doesn’t have a window in the ceiling.” The boy thought for a moment, very seriously. “So Hélène won’t be able to see us?”

Before Julien could answer, Inès turned to Yanis. “You’re so dumb,” she said, with the authority of her twelve years and her recent fame. “She doesn’t need a window. She’ll be in the waltz. Even though we can’t see her, she’s always in the waltz.” Nobody, not even Julien, found anything to add.

That evening, coming home, Julien found Ioana sitting on the living-room floor with Rose-Hélène on her lap. The little one, who would turn two in March, was tapping on the old piano with one hand, always the same three notes. Julien stopped in the doorway. He recognised the three notes. It was the beginning of the waltz.

“Since when has she been doing that?” he whispered. “Since this afternoon,” Ioana replied. “I didn’t teach her anything. She started on her own.” They stayed there, both of them, without moving, listening to their daughter play the first three notes of Henri’s waltz, again and again, while outside it gently began to snow over the Croix-Rousse. Somewhere, Julien thought, an old lady must be smiling. She had waited all her life. But her waltz no longer needed to wait for anyone.

Hello everyone, here is the press review for this Friday, 18 October. On the front page of “Lyon Matin”: “La Duchère children invited to Paris”. The paper describes how the news was announced last night, live, to a young twelve-year-old clarinettist.

According to the paper, the video of Inès’s reaction has reportedly already been viewed more than two hundred thousand times. “Mum, I looked at the camera,” she said at the end of the programme. Within a few hours the sentence became the most shared in the region.

In “Le Progrès”, another headline: “Sharp rise in enrolments at music schools”. According to the paper, applications have reportedly risen by forty per cent since the start of the school year. The Conservatoire is said to be considering setting up two new orchestras.

The La Duchère neighbourhood paper, for its part, publishes its first article signed by Marc Delorme. The young man, who in September had written a fake story about the hall, describes a Wednesday rehearsal. He admits his mistakes from the very first line.

“I thought I was writing about a scandal,” he writes. “I found sixty children who work harder than I do. Admittedly, I know nothing about music. Yet on Wednesday I understood one thing: a wrong note can be corrected. A false piece of news, much less easily.”

Finally, a brief item in the national press: “Towards a tour of children’s orchestras?” The Ministry of Culture is reportedly studying a project inspired by the Lyon experience. Nothing has been confirmed yet. Have a good day, everyone.
